analysis.body:
The U.S. Government Accountability Office found that twenty of twenty-three major federal agencies reported roughly 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, covering specific challenges or opportunities that AI may address. Of those, only about 200 instances involved AI that agencies reported as currently in production and operational use, with most use cases still in planning phases. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of AI use cases among agencies surveyed. Applications described in GAO's findings include analyzing drone photographs, processing large datasets, identifying border activities through camera and radar data, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers.

Per GAO, the federal government's AI management picture is complicated by significant gaps in the quality of reported data. Five agencies provided comprehensive information for each of their use cases, while fifteen had instances of incomplete or inaccurate data, and two agencies included AI uses that were later determined not to be AI at all. GAO also found that key governmentwide requirements have not been fully met, including the absence of guidance from the Office of Management and Budget on how agencies should acquire and use AI, and the Office of Personnel Management's failure to establish or update an occupational category for employees performing AI work. Ten of twenty-three agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, twelve implemented some but not all, and one was exempt.

On the funding side, GAO notes that the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included 1.8 billion dollars for nondefense research and development investment in AI. The General Services Administration established an AI Center of Excellence, and the Department of Commerce created a plan to develop AI technical standards, making those two agencies among the more fully compliant under the requirements GAO reviewed. Without accurate inventories and consistent acquisition guidance, GAO concluded that the government's ability to manage AI risks and benefits remains constrained.

The regulatory and legislative environment surrounding government AI use is active and expansive. Theworldofai.org tracks 3,539 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily, reflecting the volume of legislative attention being directed at AI across U.S. state governments. At the international level, the OECD.AI Policy Observatory tracks national AI strategies, public-sector initiatives, and ethical frameworks across member and partner countries, while Oxford Insights produces a Government AI Readiness Index that scores countries on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption as a standard cross-national comparison tool.

Stanford HAI's AI Index, recognized as a reference by governments and policymakers in the United States, United Kingdom, and European Union among others, tracks legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement as part of its annual government and policy analysis. The 2026 edition notes a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared governing frameworks are to manage it, and describes declining data transparency as a challenge to independent measurement precisely at a moment when such measurement is, in their framing, most critical. For any public-sector organization weighing AI deployment, the GAO record suggests that compliance infrastructure, accurate use-case documentation, and clear acquisition guidance are immediate prerequisites rather than follow-on considerations, and that the absence of those foundations is already impeding effective risk management at the federal level.
